blocks.x: We originally tested Nutribullet’s revamped base model for our “budget pick” category against the Thyme & Table model, and ultimately found its performance to be so good that we named it our best overall pick, outperforming our long-standing top pick, the Nutribullet Ultra.

What I love: This little machine punches above its weight. With a 700-watt motor, it outperformed the 1,200-watt Ultra at half the price. It produced a silky green smoothie in a single 55-second cycle and a smooth pesto in two. When we examined the pesto closely, the Ultra’s still had visible bits of pine nut, albeit they were only as small as a grain of sand. The base model’s had none.

My theory is that its slightly wider wide-mouth cup lets ingredients reach the blade more easily without getting stuck. That means faster blending and less need to stop and shake the cup between cycles.

Design-wise, the base model is sleek and straightforward. To start a blend cycle, just press the cup down into the base and twist. Suction cup feet keep the machine from bouncing around on the counter. The cup’s wider mouth makes it easy to hand-wash, though the cups, to-go lids, and blade are also top-rack dishwasher-safe.

It comes with a classic 24-ounce blending cup and a 21-ounce handled tumbler that fits in a car cupholder. The sippable lid snaps open so you won’t have to worry about it falling into your face mid-sip.

What I’d leave: There's no pulse or on-off button. The single 55-second blend mode starts automatically when you push and twist the cup into place. If you need to pulse, you’ll have to twist the cup to lock and unlock it. That push-and-twist motion is easy, but it can take a bit of pressure to lock into place. If you have mobility issues, we recommend opting for the Ultra. And unlike more premium models, it’s only available in one color.

Power: 1,200 watts
Capacity: 26 oz.
Warranty: 1-year
Included: 26 oz. cup, flip-top lid, straw

What we love: Ninja’s latest personal blender lives up to its name: It’s a powerful yet compact machine with a 1,200-watt motor that rivals that of our top pick. It has four different modes: Smoothie, Ice Crush, Blend, and Pulse. The Smoothie, Ice Crush, and Blend modes all use Ninja’s Auto iQ technology, which uses a combination of blending, pulsing, and pausing to achieve the desired result.

In testing, the BlendBoss whizzed through smoothie ingredients (including those pesky fibrous kale stems) with no trouble at all, producing the silkiest smoothie out of any of the models I tested in just one 55-second Smoothie iQ cycle. It performed well in the pesto test too; its powerful blade was more than up to the task of breaking down whole garlic cloves and leafy basil.

The base of the BlendBoss is unlike that of any other personal blender I’ve seen—bulbous and sort of donut-shaped, rather than the vertical cylinder that's become industry standard. This didn’t have any real effect on the user experience or the model’s performance, but I found the cute colors and shape to be somewhat charming. The BlendBoss comes with a single-handled blending vessel, a flip-top lid, and a straw, all of which make it more suitable for smoothies than sauces or soups.

What we’d leave: At the time of writing, the only blending vessel that’s compatible with the BlendBoss is the 26-ounce handled tumbler that’s included. While the handle is nice if you’re drinking a smoothie, it feels unnecessary when using the blender for other tasks, such as puréeing soups or blitzing sauces. What’s more, that handle is actually the BlendBoss’s biggest flaw: There’s a gap in the plastic construction that allows water to get inside the handle, and because there’s no way to detach it from the body of the cup, there’s no real way to dry any droplets that get caught.
Our editors’ personal favorite: Beast Mighty 850 Plus
